Reproductive biology of the Phaeton dragonet Synchiropus phaeton was investigated through analysis of specimens collected in the Mediterranean Sea during the early spring spawning season. At a stable water temperature of 13.8 °C [T = 13.8 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) was calculated at approximately 6.5% [GSI = approximately 6.5%]. This elevated index suggests a comparatively greater relative investment of somatic tissue into reproductive structures, possibly reflecting a strategy of batch spawning across the breeding period. Histological examination of ovarian tissue confirmed the presence of multiple cohorts of developing oocytes, consistent with an iteroparous reproductive mode. The species exhibits a determinate growth pattern, with females attaining a maximum or ultimate total length of 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters] under favorable environmental conditions, which is comparable to the upper size range observed in other Mediterranean callionymids.

Sexual maturation in the Phaeton dragonet occurs well before the attainment of maximum body size, with the onset of puberty recorded at a total length of 7.2 centimeters [Lp = 7.2 centimeters]. This length at first gonadal activation corresponds to roughly 40 percent of the ultimate length observed in adult females, a proportional relationship similar to that documented for Callionymus lyra. Individuals reaching this threshold size typically weigh approximately 2.2 grams [Wwp = approximately 2.2 grams] in terms of wet weight, representing a substantial increase from the mass recorded at the earliest life stages. The relatively modest size at which reproductive competence is achieved may facilitate early recruitment into the breeding population, thereby enhancing lifetime reproductive output despite the constraints imposed by a relatively short reproductive lifespan in the wild. Field observations indicate that both males and females undergo gonadal recrudescence in late winter, with peak spawning activity coinciding with the thermal regime of early spring.

The earliest life stages of this species begin with the hatching of pelagic eggs, a process that occurs after a brief incubation period. At the prevailing water temperature of 13.8 °C [T = 13.8 °C], the age at birth, corresponding to the moment of eclosion from the chorion, is approximately 5.5 days [ab = approximately 5.5 days] post-fertilization. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge at a very small size, with an initial wet weight at birth of 0.000051 grams [Wwb = 0.000051 grams], reflecting the minute diameter of the pelagic eggs typical of the genus. This extremely low neonatal mass imposes a narrow window for the onset of exogenous feeding, as the endogenous yolk reserves are rapidly depleted. The prolarvae are initially non-feeding and rely entirely on lecithotrophic nutrition until the mouth opens and the digestive tract becomes functional, a critical transition that usually occurs within a few days following hatching under these thermal conditions.

Longevity records for Synchiropus phaeton indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] when maintained at a water temperature of 13.8 °C [T = 13.8 °C], a duration equivalent to nearly eight years under relatively stable thermal conditions. This estimate is derived from length-frequency analysis and mark-recapture data, which suggest that the species exhibits a moderate pace of life relative to other small benthic teleosts. Individuals reaching the terminal size class are characterized by an ultimate wet weight of 26.6 grams [Wwi = 26.6 grams], a value predicted by the length-weight relationship derived from a large sample of adult females. The combination of a modest adult mass and a lifespan spanning nearly a decade is unusual among demersal fishes of comparable body size, possibly reflecting low natural mortality rates in the relatively oligotrophic habitats that this dragonet occupies across its Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic range.

Mature females in spawning condition consistently exhibit a gonadosomatic index of approximately 6.5% [GSI = approximately 6.5%], sustained throughout the breeding season at temperatures around 13.8 °C [T = 13.8 °C]. The total body mass of an average reproductively active female approaches 26.6 grams [Wwi = 26.6 grams], and the onset of spawning activity occurs once individuals have surpassed the pubertal threshold of 7.2 centimeters [Lp = 7.2 centimeters] in total length and a corresponding wet weight of 2.2 grams [Wwp = 2.2 grams]. By integrating these life-history parameters, it becomes evident that the species balances an early maturation schedule against a relatively protracted adult lifespan of nearly eight years, a strategy that may buffer against interannual variability in larval survival and food availability in the variable coastal environments it inhabits.
